text.text: Kegs out past their return date
A brewery is only as consistent as its records. Logging every brew day the same way lets you repeat a great batch and find out why a bad one went wrong.
Recipe checked; grain, hops and yeast weighed and on hand
Fermenter cleaned and sanitized; tank set to
Yeast healthy: pitch rate worked out for the batch size
Add the batch with style, brew date, planned ready date and barrels.
Record mash temperature and time, and the boil length.
Note the tank on the batch and set the tank to

cells.text: Gravity dropping; dry-hop if the recipe says
Final gravity steady on two readings two days apart
Crash cool; move to brite tank; carbonate

text.text: and the ABV. A batch that stops high may have tired yeast or too cold a tank.
Fill kegs and add each one with the batch and fill date.
; the cellar loss shows straight away.
Clean and sanitize every tank after it empties, and write the date. A tank sitting dirty for days is a contamination risk.
Taste every batch at transfer and at packaging with at least two people. Note off-flavors on the batch: diacetyl (buttery), acetaldehyde (green apple), oxidation (cardboard).

The Midnight Ledger stout packaged 6.4 of 7 barrels, a cellar loss near 9 percent. The brewer notes that the dry-hop and the transfer hose length both cost beer, and shortens the hose for the next batch.
Kegs are expensive and they wander. Tracking each one by tag saves money and helps you get them back.
Give each keg a colored tag or number that does not come off. Enter it with its size. Half barrels and sixth barrels are tracked the same way.

The Orchard Gate sixth with the purple tag has been at Birch Street Tavern past its return date. The rep picks it up with Thursday's delivery and records one empty collected.
Dirty lines make good beer taste bad. Cleaning every line every two weeks keeps the taproom pouring what the brewers made.
Every 14 days: full line clean with caustic for each tap.
Every three months: acid clean as well, and take the faucets apart.
Every new keg: wipe the coupler and faucet.

Signs a line needs cleaning sooner
Glasses rinsed cold before every pour.
Hold the glass at 45 degrees, then straighten.
One finger of foam on top.

Check the cooler at 34 to 38 degrees and the glycol chiller every week. Warm beer in the line pours foam, whatever the pressure.
Wear gloves and eye protection with line cleaner. Never mix caustic and acid. Label the cleaning bucket.

The window tap and the right rail tap are due for cleaning next. The patio tap is a day past its date and is being cleaned now, so it is out of service until the evening, and the next clean is booked two weeks out.
Selling to bars, restaurants and shops grows the brewery beyond the taproom. Clear orders, on-time deliveries and keg returns keep accounts happy.

Payment terms as agreed; often 30 days for bars, sooner for new accounts.
Accounts more than 30 days late get no new deliveries until paid.
Visit each account every month; taste the beer from their tap.
Offer to help with their line cleaning schedule.
Ask which beers sell fastest and plan brews around it.
A confirmed order whose delivery date has passed shows under Overdue. Call the account that morning with a new time; a bar that runs out of your beer puts someone else's on the tap.
Distributors order on a schedule. Plan their volume four to six weeks ahead so the tanks are free in time, and agree how they report sales by account.
Hollow Oak Grill is a new account taking four kegs this week. The rep sets payment on delivery for the first three orders and books a visit two weeks later to taste the beer on their lines.

A small brewery has beer in many places at once: in tanks, in the cooler, on tap, and at bars across town. This workspace tracks each of those, so you know what is ready, what is pouring and who has your kegs.
